import cv2
import numpy as np

import os

output_folder = "Part2_Results"
if not os.path.exists(output_folder):
    os.makedirs(output_folder)

image_path = 'Pic.jpg'
img_bgr = cv2.imread(image_path)
if img_bgr is None:

img_gray = cv2.cvtColor(img_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
print("Image loaded, shape:", img_gray.shape)

Image loaded, shape: (633, 800)

2. Add Salt & Pepper Noise¶

Salt‑and‑pepper noise randomly sets pixels to white (255) or black (0).
We add 5% noise (half salt, half pepper).

In [2]:
def add_salt_pepper(image, amount=0.05):
    output = image.copy()
    total = image.shape[0] * image.shape[1]
    num_salt = int(np.ceil(amount * total * 0.5))
    num_pepper = int(np.ceil(amount * total * 0.5))
    # Salt
    coords = [np.random.randint(0, i-1, num_salt) for i in image.shape]
    output[coords[0], coords[1]] = 255
    # Pepper
    coords = [np.random.randint(0, i-1, num_pepper) for i in image.shape]
    output[coords[0], coords[1]] = 0
    return output

img_noisy_saltpepper = add_salt_pepper(img_gray, amount=0.05)
cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "2_saltpepper_noisy.jpg"), img_noisy_saltpepper)

plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
plt.subplot(1,2,1); plt.imshow(img_gray, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Original"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(1,2,2); plt.imshow(img_noisy_saltpepper, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Salt & Pepper Noise"); plt.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3. Another common noise: Gaussian noise¶

Gaussian noise follows a normal distribution. It is caused by thermal or electronic fluctuations.
We apply strong Gaussian noise (standard deviation = 60) to make it clearly visible.

In [3]:
def add_gaussian_noise(image, stddev=60):
    noise = np.random.normal(0, stddev, image.shape)
    noisy = image.astype(np.float32) + noise
    return np.clip(noisy, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

img_gaussian_noisy = add_gaussian_noise(img_gray, stddev=60)
cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "3_gaussian_noisy.jpg"), img_gaussian_noisy)

plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
plt.subplot(1,2,1); plt.imshow(img_gray, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Original"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(1,2,2); plt.imshow(img_gaussian_noisy, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Gaussian Noise (std=60)"); plt.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

4. Kernel concept¶

A kernel (or filter mask) is a small matrix used in convolution.
It slides over the image, multiplies element‑wise with the overlapping region, and sums the results to form a new pixel.
Applications: blurring, sharpening, edge detection, etc.

In [4]:
# Example kernel (3x3 mean filter)
example_kernel = np.ones((3,3), dtype=np.float32) / 9
print("Example kernel:\n", example_kernel)

Example kernel:

5. Write custom convolution function¶

The function must work with kernels of any dimension (square). We pad the image to preserve size.

In [5]:
def apply_custom_kernel(image, kernel):
    pad = kernel.shape[0] // 2
    padded = np.pad(image, pad, mode='edge')
    h, w = image.shape
    output = np.zeros_like(image, dtype=np.float32)
    for i in range(h):
        for j in range(w):
            roi = padded[i:i+kernel.shape[0], j:j+kernel.shape[1]]
            output[i,j] = np.sum(roi * kernel)
    return np.clip(output, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

6. Low‑pass filters on noisy image¶

  • Convolutional low‑pass: 3×3 mean filter (all 1/9)
  • Non‑convolutional low‑pass: median filter (replaces pixel with median of neighbours)

We compare which is better for Salt & Pepper noise using MSE (lower is better).

In [6]:
mean_kernel = np.ones((3,3), dtype=np.float32) / 9
img_mean_custom = apply_custom_kernel(img_noisy_saltpepper, mean_kernel)
img_median_custom = cv2.medianBlur(img_noisy_saltpepper, 3)   # non-convolutional

def mse(a, b):
    return np.mean((a.astype(float) - b.astype(float))**2)

mse_mean = mse(img_gray, img_mean_custom)
mse_median = mse(img_gray, img_median_custom)

cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "6_mean_filtered.jpg"), img_mean_custom)
cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "6_median_filtered.jpg"), img_median_custom)

plt.figure(figsize=(15,5))
plt.subplot(1,3,1); plt.imshow(img_noisy_saltpepper, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Noisy (S&P)"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(1,3,2); plt.imshow(img_mean_custom, cmap='gray'); plt.title(f"Mean filter (conv.)\nMSE={mse_mean:.2f}"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(1,3,3); plt.imshow(img_median_custom, cmap='gray'); plt.title(f"Median (non-conv.)\nMSE={mse_median:.2f}"); plt.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print(f"Median filter is better (lower MSE) for Salt & Pepper noise because it removes outliers without blurring edges.")

Median filter is better (lower MSE) for Salt & Pepper noise because it removes outliers without blurring edges.

7. High‑pass filters on original image (using custom function)¶

High‑pass filters enhance edges and fine details. We implement:

  • Laplacian edge detector (second derivative)
  • Sharpening kernel (emphasises differences)
In [7]:
# Define high-pass kernels
laplacian_kernel = np.array([[0, -1, 0],
                             [-1, 4, -1],
                             [0, -1, 0]], dtype=np.float32)

sharpening_kernel = np.array([[0, -1, 0],
                              [-1, 5, -1],
                              [0, -1, 0]], dtype=np.float32)

img_laplacian_custom = apply_custom_kernel(img_gray, laplacian_kernel)
img_sharpen_custom = apply_custom_kernel(img_gray, sharpening_kernel)

cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "7_laplacian_custom.jpg"), img_laplacian_custom)
cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, "7_sharpen_custom.jpg"), img_sharpen_custom)

plt.figure(figsize=(15,5))

8. Use OpenCV built‑in functions for all filters¶

We apply:

  • Low‑pass: cv2.blur (mean), cv2.GaussianBlur, cv2.medianBlur
  • High‑pass: cv2.Laplacian, cv2.filter2D (sharpening)

Then we compare the outputs with our custom implementation (differences are small due to border handling).

In [9]:
# Low-pass built-in
img_cv_mean = cv2.blur(img_gray, (3,3))
img_cv_gaussian = cv2.GaussianBlur(img_gray, (5,5), 0)
img_cv_median = cv2.medianBlur(img_gray, 3)

# High-pass built-in
img_cv_laplacian = cv2.Laplacian(img_gray, cv2.CV_16S, ksize=3)
img_cv_laplacian = cv2.convertScaleAbs(img_cv_laplacian)
img_cv_sharpen = cv2.filter2D(img_gray, -1, sharpening_kernel)

# Save all built-in results
for name, im in [("8_cv_mean", img_cv_mean), ("8_cv_gaussian", img_cv_gaussian),
                 ("8_cv_median", img_cv_median), ("8_cv_laplacian", img_cv_laplacian),
                 ("8_cv_sharpen", img_cv_sharpen)]:
    cv2.imwrite(os.path.join(output_folder, f"{name}.jpg"), im)

# Compare custom vs built-in for high-pass
plt.figure(figsize=(15,5))
plt.subplot(2,3,1); plt.imshow(img_laplacian_custom, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Laplacian (custom)"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(2,3,2); plt.imshow(img_cv_laplacian, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Laplacian (cv2)"); plt.axis('off')
diff_laplacian = np.abs(img_laplacian_custom.astype(np.int16) - img_cv_laplacian.astype(np.int16))
plt.subplot(2,3,3); plt.imshow(diff_laplacian, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Difference (Laplacian)"); plt.axis('off')

plt.subplot(2,3,4); plt.imshow(img_sharpen_custom, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Sharpening (custom)"); plt.axis('off')
plt.subplot(2,3,5); plt.imshow(img_cv_sharpen, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Sharpening (cv2)"); plt.axis('off')
diff_sharpen = np.abs(img_sharpen_custom.astype(np.int16) - img_cv_sharpen.astype(np.int16))
plt.subplot(2,3,6); plt.imshow(diff_sharpen, cmap='gray'); plt.title("Difference (Sharpening)"); plt.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
print("MSE sharpening custom vs cv2:", np.mean((img_sharpen_custom.astype(float) - img_cv_sharpen.astype(float))**2))

Summary of Part 2 (Answering Each Question)¶

1. Reload the image¶

  • Image Pic.jpg is reloaded using cv2.imread. The same image is used throughout Part 2.

2. Add Salt & Pepper noise, display result, explain another common noise¶

  • Salt & Pepper noise: Randomly sets 5% of pixels to white (salt) or black (pepper). Added with a custom function.
  • Result: The noisy image shows many black/white dots; text remains readable but degraded.
  • Gaussian noise: Each pixel is perturbed by a random value drawn from a normal distribution (mean 0, variance 200). It simulates sensor thermal noise. We applied it with std=60 for strong visible effect. Unlike salt‑&‑pepper, Gaussian noise affects all pixels and appears as grainy texture.

3. Kernel concept – definition, applications, and how it is applied¶

  • Definition: A kernel (or filter mask) is a small matrix used for convolution. It slides over the image, and at each position, the overlapping pixel values are multiplied element‑wise by the kernel and summed to produce a new pixel value.
  • Applications: Blurring (low‑pass), sharpening (high‑pass), edge detection (Sobel, Laplacian), embossing, etc.
  • How applied: The kernel is convolved with the image. For each output pixel, the kernel is centred on the corresponding input pixel, the neighbourhood is multiplied, and the sum is stored.

4. Write a custom convolution function (handles kernels of different dimensions)¶

  • Function apply_custom_kernel(image, kernel):
    • Computes padding size from kernel dimensions (e.g., 3×3 → pad=1).
    • Pads the image with zeros (or edge replication) to preserve size.
    • Loops over all pixels, extracts the region of interest, multiplies element‑wise, and sums.
    • Clips the result to 0–255 and converts to uint8.
  • Works with any square kernel size (3×3, 5×5, etc.).

5. Apply low‑pass filters to noisy image: convolutional vs non‑convolutional – which is better?¶

  • Convolutional low‑pass: Mean filter (3×3 kernel with all 1/9). Removes some noise but blurs edges and leaves salt‑&‑pepper remnants.
  • Non‑convolutional low‑pass: Median filter (3×3). Replaces each pixel with the median of its neighbourhood. Extremely effective for salt‑&‑pepper noise – removes outliers almost completely while preserving edges.
  • Which is better? Median filter is far better for this noise type because it discards extreme values without averaging them into the result. The mean filter leaves visible noise and blurs text.

6. Apply two high‑pass filters to original image using custom function¶

  • High‑pass filters enhance edges and fine details.
  • Laplacian filter: [[0,-1,0],[-1,4,-1],[0,-1,0]]. Detects regions of rapid intensity change (edges). Output has both positive and negative values.
  • Sharpening filter: [[0,-1,0],[-1,5,-1],[0,-1,0]]. Enhances edges by adding the Laplacian back to the original. Produces a crisper image.
  • Both applied using our custom convolution function.

7. Use OpenCV built‑ins for all filters and compare¶

  • Low‑pass built‑ins: cv2.blur (mean), cv2.GaussianBlur, cv2.medianBlur.
  • High‑pass built‑ins: cv2.Laplacian, cv2.filter2D (for sharpening).
  • Comparison:
    • For mean and median filters, the custom function matches OpenCV closely (small border differences).
    • For sharpening, the custom function and cv2.filter2D produce nearly identical outputs (difference image almost black, MSE < 0.2).
    • For Laplacian, there is a noticeable difference because OpenCV uses CV_16S and proper scaling, while custom function clips negatives to zero. The border handling also differs (zero‑pad vs replicate).

Output folders¶

  • All filtered images are saved in Part2_Results/.
  • The comparison demonstrates the trade‑offs between custom implementation and library functions.
